note: Theatre parameters and sources. Same discipline as the physiology engine (Milestone 8): every parameter carries a status — cited (traceable to a consulted source below), calibrated (chosen value inside a cited range, disclosed), or verify (engineering placeholder, visibly flagged, never presented as clinical fact). The Rust loader hard-fails any parameter that is neither cited, calibrated, nor verify-flagged, exactly as physiology::Params does.

sources.carries: Primary cause of bile duct injury was a visual perceptual illusion in 97% of cases; technical faults 3%. Stewart-Way classification: class I 7%, class II 22%, class III 61%, class IV 10%. Class III mechanism: the common duct is mistaken for the cystic duct and deliberately transected. Only 25% of injuries were recognised at the index operation.
sources.cite: Way LW, Stewart L, Gantert W, et al. Causes and prevention of laparoscopic bile duct injuries: analysis of 252 cases from a human factors and cognitive psychology perspective. Ann Surg. 2003;237(4):460-469. PMID 12677139.

sources.carries: The three Critical View of Safety criteria: (1) the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue (the common bile duct and common hepatic duct do not have to be exposed); (2) the lower one-third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver to expose the cystic plate; (3) two and only two structures should be seen entering the gallbladder. The hepatocystic triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct, and the inferior edge of the liver.
sources.cite: Strasberg SM, Brunt LM. Rationale and use of the critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. J Am Coll Surg. 2010;211(1):132-138 (criteria originally Strasberg et al. 1995).

sources.carries: The critical view of safety is the preferred method of cystic duct identification. A momentary pause to confirm the CVS before clipping or transecting the cystic duct/artery. When the CVS cannot be obtained, the operative strategy should be altered, preferably to subtotal cholecystectomy (laparoscopic or open). Strong recommendations: intraoperative biliary imaging when anatomy is uncertain or injury is suspected; referral of patients with confirmed or suspected bile duct injury to an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon/team.
sources.cite: Brunt LM, Deziel DJ, Telem DA, et al. Safe cholecystectomy multi-society practice guideline and state of the art consensus conference on prevention of bile duct injury during cholecystectomy. Surg Endosc. 2020;34(7):2827-2855. PMID 32399938.

sources.carries: Subtotal cholecystectomy is the bailout when the CVS cannot be attained: it avoids dissecting the hepatocystic triangle. Fenestrating subtype: the gallbladder remnant is left open (no sealed lumen); the cystic duct is closed from inside (e.g. purse-string suture or stapler). Reconstituting subtype: the remnant is closed, reconstituting a lumen in which stones can re-form, with possible need for reoperation.
sources.cite: Strasberg SM, Pucci MJ, Brunt LM, Deziel DJ. Subtotal cholecystectomy — 'fenestrating' vs 'reconstituting' subtypes and the prevention of bile duct injury. J Am Coll Surg. 2016;222(1):89-96.

sources.carries: Cognitive task analysis expanded the laparoscopic cholecystectomy task model from 19 steps (expert recall alone) to 97 microsteps; a 'Step 0: planning the procedure' was added; dissection carried the most microsteps (15) and intraoperative cholangiogram the next most (10). Experts omit 50-70% of steps on unaided recall — the reason this procedure is authored against consulted operative sources, not recalled.
sources.cite: Villarreal ME, et al. Using a task analysis to describe the technical requirements of laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Surg Endosc. 2023;37(5):3921-3925. PMID 37036502.

sources.carries: The three checklist integration points in the procedure model and their phase placement.
sources.cite: World Health Organization. WHO Surgical Safety Checklist. 2008/2009 (19 items, three phases: Sign In before induction of anaesthesia, Time Out before skin incision, Sign Out before the patient leaves the operating room). Outcome data: Haynes AB, et al. A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. N Engl J Med. 2009;360:491-499 (death rate 1.5% to 0.8%; inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0%).

sources.carries: Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g for patients weighing >=120 kg), started within 60 minutes before surgical incision; redosing interval 4 hours.
sources.cite: Bratzler DW, Dellinger EP, Olsen KM, et al. Clinical practice guidelines for antimicrobial prophylaxis in surgery. Am J Health-Syst Pharm. 2013;70(3):195-283.

sources.carries: GOALS: five domains (depth perception, bimanual dexterity, efficiency, tissue handling, autonomy), each rated 1-5 with descriptive anchors at 1, 3 and 5; total 25. Ships in the procedure's scoring block as rubric data for observed-performance rating; a headless scripted runner cannot populate it (see scoring.notes).
sources.cite: Vassiliou MC, Feldman LS, Andrew CG, et al. A global assessment tool for evaluation of intraoperative laparoscopic skills. Am J Surg. 2005;190(1):107-113.

sources.carries: OSATS global rating scale: seven items (respect for tissue, time and motion, instrument handling, knowledge of instruments, use of assistants, flow of operation, knowledge of specific procedure), each 1-5; total 35. Rubric data only in v1, for the same reason as GOALS.
sources.cite: Martin JA, Regehr G, Reznick R, et al. Objective structured assessment of technical skill (OSATS) for surgical residents. Br J Surg. 1997;84(2):273-276 (global rating items as reproduced in subsequent validation literature).

sources.carries: Debrief structure: Setting the Scene, Reactions, Description, Analysis, Summary. The Analysis phase blends three strategies matched to the performance gap: learner self-assessment (plus-delta), focused facilitation (including advocacy-inquiry), and directive feedback/teaching. The runner's debrief emits Description from the event log, Analysis as plus/delta/directive entries, and a Summary; Setting the Scene and Reactions are facilitator acts in live use and are labelled as such.
sources.cite: Eppich W, Cheng A. Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS): development and rationale for a blended approach to health care simulation debriefing. Simul Healthc. 2015;10(2):106-115. PMID 25710312.

sources.carries: Double cystic artery prevalence 13% (95% CI 11-16%); cystic artery absent in 2% (CI 1-4%); cystic artery origin from the right hepatic artery in 89% (CI 85-92%); mean cystic artery length 20.77 mm, mean diameter 1.91 mm. Basis of the second procedure variant and of the order-of-magnitude anchor for the cystic bleed placeholder.
sources.cite: Asghar K, et al. Double cystic artery: a meta-analysis. Clin Ter. 2024;175(3):184-192. DOI 10.7417/CT.2024.5061. PMID 38767077.

sources.carries: Port placement, retraction directions, window creation, extraction and closure microsteps.
sources.cite: Operative technique references consulted in-session: standard four-port 'American' configuration operative descriptions (10 mm infraumbilical camera port; 10 mm epigastric port placed about 2 cm below the liver edge to the right of the falciform ligament; 5 mm mid-clavicular and 5 mm anterior-axillary working ports; fundus retracted cephalad over the liver dome; infundibulum retracted caudolaterally; windows created between cystic duct and cystic artery and between cystic artery and liver edge before division; specimen extracted in a retrieval bag via the umbilical port; fascial closure at 10 mm port sites).
